result:
**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my stomach like a stone.

I didn’t know then that some sentences are boulders, that they can sit in you for years, pressing against your ribs every time you take a deep breath.

II.

There’s a myth that writers are born with an overflowing well of ideas, that we wake up with sentences already formed on our tongues. The truth is messier. Most days, I sit in front of a blank page and feel like a fraud. The cursor blinks at me, judgmental. *Why aren’t you saying something important?* it seems to ask. As if importance is something you can summon like a spell.

I once read that Hemingway said, *"There is nothing to writing. All you do is sit down at a typewriter and bleed."* But what if you’re all dried up? What if you’ve spent so long squeezing out words that there’s nothing left but the echo of them?

III.

I had a friend in college who believed in the power of manifesting. She would write her desires on slips of paper—*I will fall in love this year*, *I will get the job*—and burn them under the full moon. "The universe listens," she’d say. I never told her that the universe had never answered me, not even when I whispered *Please* into the dark as a child, not even when I begged it to make my mother’s illness go away.

Words, I learned, are not magic. They are tools. Sometimes they build. Sometimes they destroy. And sometimes, no matter how hard you throw them into the void, they just… disappear.

IV.

Have you ever loved someone so much that their name felt like a prayer? I did. His was *Daniel*, two syllables that tasted like honey and hurt going down. I wrote him letters I never sent, filled with things I was too afraid to say out loud. *I think about you when I’m supposed to be working. I memorized the way your laugh sounds in a crowded room. I am terrified you’ll see how much I need you and run.*

Love, like writing, is an act of vulnerability. You hand someone your heart and hope they don’t drop it. But people are careless with fragile things.

V.

The internet has turned words into currency. We trade them for likes, for attention, for the fleeting high of being *seen*. We reduce complex emotions to 280 characters. We argue in comment sections, hurling sentences like weapons, forgetting that on the other side of the screen is a person who might also be lonely, who might also be hurting.

I wonder sometimes if we’ve lost the art of silence. If we’ve forgotten that not every thought needs to be spoken, that some things are better left unsaid.

VI.

My grandmother used to say, *"Words are like teeth—once they’re out, you can’t put them back in."* She had a way of speaking in proverbs, as if life could be distilled into neat, digestible lessons. But life isn’t neat. Neither are words. They spill out of us in messy, contradictory bursts. *I love you. I hate you. I don’t know who I am without you.*

VII.

I used to keep a journal under my bed. It was filled with the kind of dramatic, self-important musings only a teenager could produce. *No one understands me. The world is ending. I will never be happy.* Reading it now, I cringe. But I also ache for that girl, for the way she believed her pain was unique, that no one had ever felt so deeply before.

We all think we’re the first to discover heartbreak. The first to stare into the abyss. The first to wonder if we’re doing this whole *being human* thing wrong.

VIII.

There’s a Japanese concept called *mono no aware*—the pathos of things, the bittersweet awareness of impermanence. It’s the feeling you get when you see cherry blossoms fall, or when you hold a child’s hand and realize they won’t always need you. Words, too, are impermanent. They fade from memory. They get lost in translation. They change meaning over time.

I used to think I could write my way into immortality. Now I know that even the greatest stories eventually turn to dust.

IX.

What do you do with the words that don’t fit anywhere? The ones that are too raw for poetry, too fragmented for essays, too honest for small talk? I collect them in the notes app on my phone, a graveyard of half-formed thoughts. *Why does grief feel like a stone in my throat? How do people decide to stay? I don’t recognize myself in the mirror anymore.*

Maybe one day I’ll turn them into something. Or maybe they’ll stay there, silent and heavy, like all the things I’ve never said.

X.

I have 1000 words. I’ve used 997.

The last three are for you:

*You are not alone.*
